name_en: Pamukkale travertine terraces and thermal springs
name_tr_source: OSM way 15494594 name:tr; Wikidata Q123014534

footprint.osm_polygon_way_15494594: oriented bbox approx. 1374 x 673 m, long axis ~156 deg (NNW-SSE) - mapped tourist/protected terrace zone, not the full geological deposit
footprint.literature: travertine formation in total about 2,700 m long, 600 m wide and 160 m high (Wikipedia/Pamukkale); UNESCO: springs emerge from a cliff almost 200 m high

period: Natural; deposited over millennia by calcite-laden hot springs; the springs drew visitors from antiquity (spa from at least the 2nd c. BC)
phases: Natural deposition, ongoing
Ancient spa use from Hellenistic period
Modern hotels built on the terraces later removed; water flow now regulated and sections closed for regeneration

key_facts.fact: UNESCO: calcite-laden waters from springs in a cliff almost 200 m high created 'mineral forests, petrified waterfalls and a series of terraced basins'; Pamukkale means 'Cotton Palace/Castle'.
Hierapolis-Pamukkale was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1988 under criteria (iii)(iv)(vii); property 1,077 ha.
17 hot springs with temperatures of 35-100 C feed the area; water emerging from the spring is carried 320 m to the head of the terraces.
When the CaCO3-supersaturated water reaches the surface, CO2 degasses and calcium carbonate is deposited as a soft gel that crystallises into travertine.
UNESCO notes the springs feed a hydraulic system extending 70 km north-west to Alasehir and west along the Menderes valley, and were used in antiquity for scouring and drying wool.

disputed: Dimensions of the travertine body (2,700 x 600 x 160 m) come from Wikipedia without a primary geological citation - verify before quoting.
Spring temperature range (35-100 C) is from Wikipedia; the Antique Pool spring is about 36 C (various sources).
coord_uncertainty: Area feature; point is a representative viewpoint, not a centroid of the geology.

key_facts.fact: Triple-arched gate of squared travertine blocks flanked by two round towers, recalling Hellenistic gates such as Perge.
Built by the proconsul Julius Frontinus (AD 84-86) and dedicated to Domitian.
A bilingual (Latin/Greek) inscription on the gate names Sextus Julius Frontinus.
Beside the gate stands the Tomb of Flavius Zeuxis, a textile merchant whose inscription says he made 72 sea voyages (to Italy).
Humann's 1887 survey drew the north gate and colonnaded street at 1:1500 (Altertümer von Hierapolis, 1898).

Frontinus Street was originally 14 m wide, named after Sextus Julius Frontinus (AD 86), and narrowed in the early Byzantine period.
The Hellenistic city was laid out on a grid with streets parallel or perpendicular to the main thoroughfare.
Shops, a latrine and the Nymphaeum of the Tritons line the excavated northern stretch (OSM mapping and site panels).

key_facts.fact: The necropolis extends over 2 km and affords a vast panorama of Greco-Roman funerary practice.
About 1,200 tombs; over 300 inscriptions read; mostly 2nd c. BC - 3rd c. AD.
Tomb types: simple graves, sarcophagi (often on podia), circular tumuli with dromos and vaulted chamber, and temple-like family tombs.
Tomb 163D is an early-1st-c. AD Jewish family tomb; Tomb 148B carries a menorah - evidence of the Jewish community.
The sarcophagus of Marcus Aurelius Ammianos, with the relief of a water-powered stone sawmill (earliest known crank-and-connecting-rod machine, 2nd half 3rd c. AD), comes from this necropolis.
Iron Age round huts were found in 2016 excavations at the park entrance in the Northern Necropolis area.

disputed: Tomb count 'about 1,200' is widely repeated; the Italian Nuovo Atlante (2015) is the authoritative catalogue - not consulted here.

key_facts.fact: The North Agora (280 x 170 m) was built during the 2nd c. AD; single-storey porticoes on three sides.
The Stoa-basilica on the E side rose on a monumental stair 5 m high and 280 m long; dated late Hadrianic-early Antonine; a statue base dedicated to Antoninus Pius was found in its propylon collapse.
Capitals with lions attacking bulls and Ionic capitals with masks come from the Antonine Stoa-basilica.
The Agora was largely destroyed by a 4th-c. earthquake; its stone was reused for the city walls.
It may have hosted gladiatorial shows on occasion (Sacchi, citing earlier studies).

key_facts.fact: Under Septimius Severus the old scaenae frons was replaced by a three-storey one flanked by two side buildings, decorated with mythological reliefs and dedicatory inscriptions.
A relief shows Septimius Severus with Julia Domna, Caracalla, Geta and Jupiter; friezes depict cycles of Apollo and Artemis and a festival of Dionysus.
UNESCO highlights the Severan theatre's frieze of a ritual procession and sacrifice to the Ephesian Artemis.
The orchestra was probably converted in AD 352 for aquatic shows.
Collapsed in the 7th-c. earthquake; a recurring subject for European travellers' engravings from the 18th c.; restored 2004-2014.
Humann's 1887 survey produced a 1:750 plan of the theatre.

name_en: Temple of Apollo (Sanctuary of Apollo Lairbenos)
name_tr_source: OSM way 116720715 name:tr; official panel 'APOLLON KUTSAL ALANI' (OSM node 11800284625)

key_facts.fact: Dedicated to Apollo Lairbenos, the city's principal god, linked with the Anatolian sun god Lairbenos and the oracle god Kareios.
Built, like the Ploutonion, on the surface trace of a seismic fault revered as a gateway of Hades (Piccardi, CNR, 1998 study).
UNESCO: the Temple of Apollo, which includes several chthonian divinities, was erected on a geological fault from which noxious vapours escaped.
Rebuilt in the 3rd c. AD in Roman fashion reusing blocks from the older temple; only the marble floor of the reconstruction remains.

name_tr_source: Official bilingual site panel 'PLOUTONION (CEHENNEM KAPISI)' transcribed in OSM node 11800249343; Wikidata Q139435613 'Hierapolis Plütonyum'

footprint.literature: cave chamber about 3 m2; an enclosed area of 2,000 m2 in front of the entrance (Wikipedia, from ancient descriptions)

period: Phrygian/Archaic cult origin; monumental phase 2nd half of 1st c. AD (Neronian-Flavian, after AD 60 earthquake)
phases: Ia Archaic (Phrygian): stepped altar carved in the rock above the cave
Ib Hellenistic: temenos and Doric portico on N side
IIa Augustan/Julio-Claudian: facade with Ionic semi-columns framing the cave; theatron on E side
IIb Neronian and after (post-AD 60 earthquake): monumentalisation - Ionic portico and sacellum housing the colossal marble Hades statue, tholos, theatron extended N and S, abaton
IIIa Imperial: Stoa of the Springs to the S; monumental entrance N of the temenos
IIIb Late Roman: repairs after 4th-c. earthquake; votive deposits
IV Early Byzantine (5th-7th c.): sanctuary obliterated, residential district built over it
V Middle Byzantine (9th-10th c.): houses and olive-processing facility (molae oleariae)
VI 10th-early 11th c.: collapse of Wall A in a powerful earthquake
VII Seljuq (12th-14th c.) and later: frequented by nomadic herders

key_facts.fact: Strabo: 'Any animal that passes inside meets instant death. I threw in sparrows and they immediately breathed their last and fell.'

Excavations began in 2008 under the Italian mission; the discovery was announced by Francesco D'Andria (Univ. of Salento) in Istanbul in March 2013: a temple, a pool, steps above the gas-emitting cave, and a dedication to Pluto and Kore.
In 2013 two marble statues - Cerberus and a coiled snake - were found in the thermal springs; they had been damaged in the 4th-6th c., probably by Christian pilgrims.

Pfanz et al. measured CO2 up to 91% inside the grotto and 4-53% near the mouth depending on height; the gas pools at night and is strongest at dawn, explaining why sacrificed animals died while taller priests survived.
Castrated priests of Cybele (Galli) were said to enter the cave unharmed; priests sold birds to visitors to test the gas.
A replica of the Hades-and-Cerberus statue has been placed at its original position.

disputed: Two locations have been called 'Ploutonion': the cave by the Temple of Apollo (identified in the 1960s; Wikidata Q12901539 coordinates point here, ~80 m NW of OSM relation) and the sanctuary ~ to the SE excavated 2008-2013 with the dedicatory inscription. Use the OSM relation for the 2013 sanctuary.
Discovery year: '1965' (Wikipedia, for the cave by the Apollo temple) vs 2013 (announcement of the sanctuary).
Whether priests performed sacrifices at dawn (Pfanz) or at night (D'Andria, oil lamps) is debated.
coord_uncertainty: Wikidata Q12901539 is offset ~80 m from OSM relation - reflects the older identification.

UNESCO flags the pool as particularly threatened: swimming causes biological pollution and erosion of ancient marble.

The tomb, empty of relics, stood at the centre of a three-naved basilica (Church of the Sepulchre); Greek prayers venerating Philip are carved on tomb and church walls.
A 6th-c. bread stamp (signum pistoris) shows Philip; pilgrims reached the hill along a processional street identified in 2008.
Tomb chamber 3.50 x 4 m with three stone benches; church unearthed in 2011.
